subject: bug in stan with geometric series

messages.author: 97d82fedb7016adb
messages.subject: bug in stan with geometric series
parts:
Hi!

I am developing a model for which I need to sum up exp(-k * t) terms. This summation is done in the transformed parameters block. To speed up things I decided to represent this as geometric series. However, if you do that, then Stan does very weird things. It looks like Stan can not correctly auto-differentiate the term

1-pow(exp(-k * t), 100)/(1 - exp(-k * t))

with k being 0.05 or so and t=50. Is it possible that stan is choking on the very small number which is the result of taking the power 100 of the exponential?

Many thanks in advance!

Best,
Sebastian

exp(log_sum_exp(my_vector))

anyway, where my_vector contains the -k * t stuff.

Ben

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: bug in stan with geometric series
parts:
On 5/3/13 3:03 AM, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi Bob!
>
> Thanks for pointing out this function.
That was Ben, not me!

> I reformulated my expressions using the above rationale like this:
>
> sad <- exp(log_sum_exp(0, -ka * TAU)) - 2;
> sadn <- exp(log_sum_exp(0, -ka * nd * TAU)) - 2;
> sadf <- exp(log(-1*sadn) - log(-1*sad));

Here are some more helpful functions:

log1p_exp(u) =def= log_sum_exp(0, u)

Also note that log(-1 * v) == log(-v).

How do you guarantee that sadn < -0 and sad < 0 so
that the log works in the definition of sadf? See
the comment down at the bottom.

The -2 is going to be problematic anyway, as it
forces you out of the log scale.

Here's a general post about how and why to use log_sum_exp:

https://hips.seas.harvard.edu/blog/2013/01/09/computing-log-sum-exp/

> Very ugly, but it seems to work.
> If someone is aware of more elegant solution, I would appreciate it.

I'm afraid there's really no way around it for these
kinds of operations. Even if you change the scale of
the data or parameters, it's still better to use log_sum_exp.
We build a lot of this kind of thing into the distributions
(such as using a poisson_log(x) instead of poisson(exp(x))).
And we're always looking for suggestions to make it better.

But if you do your own arithmetic, you can still run into
arithmetic problems.

> It looks to me I
> am experiencing numerical instabilities.

Almost certainly numerical issues given the scale of the numbers
and operations you're using.

> Are there any guidelines around for what are good and bad practice expressions
> in the context of autdiff stuff?

It's not autodiff per se, but just basic floating point
arithmetic. Which can be very subtle and which I'm still
coming to grips with.

The guidelines for Stan are basically the same as for any
other numerical software. Unfortunately, there are a huge
number of guidelines --- whole books just introducing
the numerical subtleties of basic arithmetic, then more
books on matrix algebra, whole papers on special functions
like gamma, etc. etc. etc. Ben knows the most about the
matrix algebra issues, but none of us are numerical analysts.

Tip 1. Always work on the log scale if you can to prevent
overflow and underflow that would arise on the natural scale.
For example, don't take the product of a bunch of probabilities,
take the sum of the logs.

Tip 2. Avoid catastrophic cancellation in subtraction

You can put tip 1 and tip 2 together and use

log1m(x) =def= log(1 - x)

Autodiff is rarely the problem if the operators and
themselves don't have arithmetic problems. Autodiff just
involves the evaluation of analytic derivatives by
tracing through the program.

For instance, if you have exp(x), then the derivative
is exp(x), and both have exactly the same stability issues
(x < -700 or so underflows; x > 700 or so overflows).
If the expression is log(x), the derivative is 1/x.
1/x produces extreme values if x is extreme.

One extra subtlety for us is that there are implicit
exponentiations in places. For instance, if you declare
a variable positive (lower=0) then there's an implicit exp()
applied to map the unconstrained parameter back to the
positive numbers.

> However, once I done this I run into another bizarre problem:
>
> Error : No acceptably small step size could be found. Perhaps the posterior is not continuous?
> error occurred during calling the sampler; sampling not done
>
> I know that I handle very small quantities in my problem - does it mean I have to switch to log scale on all my
> computations? Or can I force Stan to use a certain lower step size?

You can initialize the step size or just set it outright.
But this error message means no step size is small enough to move
from the current parameter value to another parameter value in
support. This usually happens if you initialize somewhere outisde
of the support of the log probability function. For instance, if one of your
sad or sadn isn't negative.

It can also come up if you're very close to a constraint boundary,
like positive definiteness for covariance matrices.

You might want to try the dump of derivatives if the problem's
not too large (it uses finite differences, which can be slow in
large dimensions). If the log probability is NaN or -infinity,
the initialization point is out of support. (Be
warned --- the dump is on the unconstrained scale.)

- Bob

Stan shouldn't crash even if there is some bug in your code. You probably just have to attack it with gdb but make sure to first either do set_cppo("debug") from RStan or from command-line Stan add -g to CFAGS in the makefile and compile with O=0.

On 5/4/13 10:10 AM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> On Saturday, May 4, 2013 9:44:01 AM UTC-4, Sebastian Weber wrote:

> if stan or (again) me is causing the trouble. Any hints where I can search? I am not shy to use gdb to dig into it,
> but anything I can do before going this far. Have there been some patches around log1m lately?
>
> Stan shouldn't crash even if there is some bug in your code. You probably just have to attack it with gdb but make sure
> to first either do set_cppo("debug") from RStan or from command-line Stan add -g to CFAGS in the makefile and compile
> with O=0.

There aren't any issues with log1m(x) of which we're
aware --- if x > 1, we'll throw an exception, but RStan
should be trapping that if you're running in "debug" mode.
One thing you might try is printing the x before calling
log1m to see if that's what's happening. You can even
say something like

if (x > 1) print("bad x for log1m(x), x=", x);

Are you using set_cppo("debug")? If so, and RStan
is still crashing, that's a bug in RStan, and we'd
really appreciate it if you could send us the full model
and data (or even better, a smaller model where we
can reproduce the error).

Jiqiang/Ben: what's the default mode with RStan?

I think what makes most sense is to have two modes:

standard: -O3, check bounds, never crashes R (i.e., trap all exceptions)

fast: -O3, no bounds checks, may crash R

When somebody sets "fast" mode we should indicate that
(a) how much faster they can expect things to go, and (b) that
they're running the risk of crashing R and losing their
environment.

It may also make sense to have a third option if there's
some reason to ever compile with -O0:

debug: -O0, +debug, check bounds, trap all exceptions

The problem with that is that we can't compile with -O0 in
Windows -- it blows out the gcc's memory.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: bug in stan with geometric series
parts:
On Saturday, May 4, 2013 3:12:22 PM UTC-4, Bob Carpenter wrote:
Jiqiang/Ben:  what's the default mode with RStan?

I think what makes most sense is to have two modes:

   standard: -O3, check bounds, never crashes R (i.e., trap all exceptions)

   fast:     -O3, no bounds checks, may crash R
Default is essentially what you call "standard", but is actually enforced with a NDEBUG argument to set_cppo() that defaults to FALSE. I actually like your way better.

When somebody sets "fast" mode we should indicate that
(a) how much faster they can expect things to go, and (b) that
they're running the risk of crashing R and losing their
environment.

It spits out b). We don't know a). We've fallen behind on speed testing, but I really wouldn't know how to guess a) unless we can somehow know how many accesses of individual elements there are and multiply that by the number of ms that the check takes and multiply that by the expected number of evaluations of the log posterior. I also think that fast mode should turn off the check for positive definiteness and maybe some other things.

It may also make sense to have a third option if there's
some reason to ever compile with -O0:

   debug:   -O0, +debug, check bounds, trap all exceptions
That option already exists.

The problem with that is that we can't compile with -O0 in
Windows -- it blows out the gcc's memory.

I think you have to do both -O0 and -g or add -mtune=native or something. Last I checked -O0 alone would work. In any event, I don't think there is gdb for Windows so it is not as if they can debug it, and debug mode is useful for !Windows with gdb or lldb.

Ben

Hi!

Finally...problem solved! To summarize: My equations rely on certain parameters being smaller than 0 otherwise bad things happen. Now, I did enforce this correctly for the group parameter, but individual subjects were allowed to violate these constrains. Once I realized this and fixed it, my model just runs fine!

Concerning the memory issues I encountered: I checked the code and saw quite a number of new operators in the stan::agrad::log1p functions. I think what happened is that I triggered with a x>1 in log1m an exception which caused the normal program flow to be aborted and ultimately some things did go wrong in this case with memory management. But I am only guessing here. BTW, is it really necessary to program stuff with pointers and new operators? I learned many times to stay away from these things...

Thanks for your support!

Sebastian

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: bug in stan with geometric series
parts:
On 5/5/13 2:07 PM, Sebastian Weber wrote:
> Hi!
>
> I will do the backtrace and post it. Concerning pointers: Why not use shared_ptr or unique_ptr c++ facilities?
> Performance reasons? These are usually much safer to use - at least I came to this conclusion for my own programming.

Yes, performance. We use an arena-based memory management
strategy where we allocate blocks of memory, use them for auto-dif,
then free them all at once.

You can think of what we're doing as implementing something
like the shared_ptr or unique_ptr in that we use a pointer
to implementation (PIMPL) idiom for the client code (stan::agrad::var).
You see the same kind of pointer/memory abstraction underlying
std::vector and Eigen::Matrix.

We've specialized operator new for our vari classes for
reverse-mode auto-dif. Then we free the memory all at once
after a gradient calculation.

The bug that's in there now, I believe, is that we're
not properly freeing memory related to a gradient calc when
we hit an exception. So we don't have a strict
resource allocation is initialization (RIAA) pattern for
our client code, which is very dangerous.

- Bob
